## What it is

When your data come in natural batches, such as survey years, countries, schools or experiments, fit the *same* model to each batch separately. Then plot the coefficient of interest from every fit side by side, with its uncertainty interval. The result is a picture of how the estimate varies across batches.

Gelman calls it the secret weapon "because it seems to be done much less often than it could be. I suspect the technique is not used more because people are fixated on point estimates and don't realize that a graph can tell a clearer story." He also describes it as "an approximation to multilevel modeling, with the partial pooling done by eye on the graphs rather than using a full statistical model." It needs no new methodology, just a loop and a graph.

## Why it matters

A single model fit to pooled data gives you one number and hides everything else. Do the batches agree? Is there a trend over time? Is one batch an outlier driving the result? Fitting separately and plotting together answers these questions at a glance. It is also an honest first step before building a [multilevel model](mister-p.qmd): the plot shows you whether, and how much, pooling is warranted.

## How it works

1. Split the data by the batching variable $g = 1, \dots, G$.
2. Fit $y_i = \alpha_g + \beta_g x_i + \epsilon_i$ in each batch and record $\hat\beta_g$ and its standard error.
3. Plot $\hat\beta_g \pm 1\,\text{se}$ against $g$. Year on the x-axis is the classic choice.
4. Look for structure. A smooth trend suggests modeling $\beta_g$ as a function of time. Scatter consistent with the error bars suggests the batches share a common coefficient.

## Simulated example

A survey is run every two years from 1972 to 2024, and in each year we regress an outcome on a predictor. The true coefficient drifts smoothly over time. Try shrinking the per-year sample size: each estimate becomes noisier, but the trend is still visible across the whole set.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {rng, range, lm} from "../js/stats.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof nPerYear = Inputs.range([20, 2000], {value: 300, step: 10, label: "Respondents per survey"})
viewof trend = Inputs.radio(["Rising", "Flat", "Rise and fall"], {value: "Rising", label: "True pattern"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 11, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
fits = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  const years = range(27).map(i => 1972 + 2 * i);
  const truth = yr => {
    const t = (yr - 1972) / 52;
    return trend === "Rising" ? 0.1 + 0.5 * t : trend === "Flat" ? 0.3 : 0.1 + 1.2 * t * (1 - t) * 1.6;
  };
  return years.map(year => {
    const beta = truth(year);
    const x = r.normals(nPerYear);
    const y = x.map(v => 1 + beta * v + r.normal(0, 1));
    const f = lm(x, y);
    return {year, beta, est: f.b, lo: f.b - f.seB, hi: f.b + f.seB};
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  ariaLabel: "The Secret Weapon: simulation chart",
  ariaDescription: "Horizontal axis: Survey year. Vertical axis: Estimated coefficient (±1 se). The chart updates with the controls above it, and the summary below the charts states the result in words.",
  height: 320,
  y: {label: "Estimated coefficient (±1 se)", grid: true},
  x: {label: "Survey year", tickFormat: "d"},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX(fits, {x: "year", y1: "lo", y2: "hi", stroke: "#2166ac"}),
    Plot.dot(fits, {x: "year", y: "est", fill: "#2166ac"}),
    Plot.line(fits, {x: "year", y: "beta", stroke: "#d6604d", strokeDasharray: "5 3"}),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const inside = fits.filter(d => d.lo <= d.beta && d.beta <= d.hi).length;
  return html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`The dashed red line is the true coefficient. With **${nPerYear}** respondents per survey, **${inside} of ${fits.length}** ±1 se intervals cover the truth (about 68% is expected). No single year tells you the trend, but the set of years does.`}</div>`;
}
```

## R {.unlisted}

```{.r}
# The Secret Weapon: fit the same model to each year, then plot them all.
n_per_year <- 300 # respondents per survey # <1>
trend <- "Rising" # or "Flat", "Rise and fall"
set.seed(11) # <2>

years <- seq(1972, 2024, by = 2)
truth <- function(yr) { # <3>
  t <- (yr - 1972) / 52
  switch(trend,
    Rising = 0.1 + 0.5 * t,
    Flat = 0.3 + 0 * t,
    "Rise and fall" = 0.1 + 1.2 * t * (1 - t) * 1.6
  )
}
fits <- t(sapply(years, function(year) { # <4>
  x <- rnorm(n_per_year)
  y <- 1 + truth(year) * x + rnorm(n_per_year)
  summary(lm(y ~ x))$coefficients["x", 1:2] # estimate and se
}))
inside <- abs(fits[, 1] - truth(years)) <= fits[, 2] # <5>
cat(
  sum(inside), "of", length(years), "intervals (+/- 1 se) cover the",
  "true coefficient\n"
)

plot(years, fits[, 1], # <6>
  pch = 19,
  ylim = range(fits[, 1] - fits[, 2], fits[, 1] + fits[, 2]),
  xlab = "Year", ylab = "Coefficient estimate"
)
segments(years, fits[, 1] - fits[, 2], years, fits[, 1] + fits[, 2])
lines(years, truth(years), col = "#d6604d", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
```
1. The page's controls: respondents per survey and the true pattern over time.
2. Fixes the random numbers so the run is reproducible.
3. The true coefficient in each year.
4. The secret weapon: fit the same regression separately to each year's survey and keep the coefficient and its standard error.
5. How many of the one-standard-error intervals cover the truth (about two thirds is expected).
6. All the estimates plotted together against the true trend. No single year shows the pattern; the set of years does.

## Python {.unlisted}

```{.python}
# The Secret Weapon: fit the same model to each year, then plot them all.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

n_per_year = 300  # respondents per survey
trend = "Rising"  # or "Flat", "Rise and fall"
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)

years = np.arange(1972, 2025, 2)


def truth(yr):
    t = (yr - 1972) / 52
    return {"Rising": 0.1 + 0.5 * t, "Flat": 0.3 + 0 * t,
            "Rise and fall": 0.1 + 1.2 * t * (1 - t) * 1.6}[trend]


est, se = [], []
for year in years:
    x = rng.normal(size=n_per_year)
    y = 1 + truth(year) * x + rng.normal(size=n_per_year)
    (b, a), cov = np.polyfit(x, y, 1, cov="unscaled")
    resid = y - (a + b * x)
    est.append(b)
    se.append(np.sqrt(cov[0, 0] * resid @ resid / (n_per_year - 2)))
est, se = np.array(est), np.array(se)
inside = np.abs(est - truth(years)) <= se
print(f"{inside.sum()} of {len(years)} intervals (+/- 1 se) cover the "
      "true coefficient")

plt.errorbar(years, est, yerr=se, fmt="o", color="black")
plt.plot(years, truth(years), "--", color="#d6604d", linewidth=2)
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("Coefficient estimate")
plt.show()
```

## Key takeaways

::: takeaways
- Fit the same model to each batch, then plot all the estimates together. It's cheap and it shows a lot.
- The display shows variation over time or across groups that a single pooled estimate hides.
- It is a natural stepping stone to a multilevel model that partially pools across batches.
:::
